blocks.title: Why Reranking for Better Answers matters in a real product

spans.text: Problem statement:

A team is dealing with a retriever finds many plausible docs and a reranker must put the truly useful evidence first. They do not need trivia about Reranking for Better Answers; they need a decision they can make, a concrete artifact they can inspect, and a way to know whether relevant evidence in the top three chunks is improving.

This lesson keeps one running case in view: reranking experiment with baseline top-k, reranked top-k, and answer quality checks. Every module asks what the system sees, what it changes, what can go wrong, and how a reviewer would prove the behavior before trusting it.

Before reading on, predict: if reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents, which part of the design would you inspect first - input, mechanism, decision rule, implementation, or monitoring?
Because this is an intermediate lesson, assume the vocabulary is learnable and spend your effort on tradeoffs, integration points, and the tests that prove the design works.

items.text: Business framing: Reranking for Better Answers matters when it changes a launch, buy/build, safety, or quality decision for the product team.
Engineering framing: Reranking for Better Answers matters when it changes state, interfaces, tests, traces, data, model behavior, or runtime limits.
Validation framing: the lesson is not done until relevant evidence in the top three chunks can be measured on examples that look like the real workload.

blocks.title: Case study: the first review meeting

spans.text: The team reviews reranking experiment with baseline top-k, reranked top-k, and answer quality checks after a week of prototype use. One user-visible metric is improving: relevant evidence in the top three chunks. But a reviewer finds the known failure pattern: reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents.

The decision is not to throw away the prototype. The team keeps the working slice, then adds one missing control: better state capture, stricter retrieval, a clearer schema, a human approval step, or a monitoring alert depending on the failure.

items.text: What changed: the artifact now records the evidence it used, not just the final answer.
What stayed small: the team did not optimize the entire stack before proving the failure could be detected.
What got measured: relevant evidence in the top three chunks became part of the release gate, not an after-the-fact dashboard.

blocks.title: Design choices: the applied idea

spans.text: The design choice is rarely "use Reranking for Better Answers" or "do not use it." The real choice is how much rigor to add for this user's risk, data, and operational burden.

In the running case, a thin slice is useful only if it proves the hardest assumption. Production design is justified when users depend on the behavior. Advanced optimization comes later, after traces show the bottleneck or failure pattern.

items.text: Choose the thin slice when the requirement is still uncertain and you need fast feedback.
Choose the production path when the failure would affect users, money, compliance, or trust.
Choose advanced optimization only after measured evidence shows the baseline is the limiting factor.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The happy path for Reranking for Better Answers is not enough. In the running case, watch for failures that look successful until a user, auditor, or downstream system checks the details.

items.text: Silent success: the system returns an answer or artifact but hides that evidence was missing, stale, or incomplete.
Wrong abstraction: the team optimizes a model, framework, or metric when the real problem is data quality, policy, state, or workflow ownership.
Evaluation gap: tests cover polished examples but not the known failure case: reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents.
Operational drift: the design works once, then degrades when traffic, data, users, or dependencies change.

spans.text: Specific diagnostic: when relevant evidence in the top three chunks worsens, inspect the first step where evidence enters the system and the last step where the output is validated.

blocks.title: Runnable check: rank evidence before generating an answer
blocks.code:
# Reranking for Better Answers: tiny retrieval check for the running case.
query = "refund deadline policy"
docs = [
    {"id": "policy-refunds", "text": "Refund requests must include the invoice id and arrive within 30 days."},
    {"id": "brand-tone", "text": "Support replies should be warm, short, and direct."},
    {"id": "shipping", "text": "Shipping delays can be escalated after 7 days."},
]

def score(doc, query):
    terms = set(query.split())
    return sum(1 for term in terms if term in doc["text"].lower())

ranked = sorted(docs, key=lambda d: score(d, query), reverse=True)
print(ranked[0]["id"])
print("grounded" if score(ranked[0], query) >= 2 else "needs review")

spans.text: This is not the full production implementation of Reranking for Better Answers. It is a runnable miniature that makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision, output, and a check tied to the running failure mode.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the two printed lines. Which document wins, and does the toy check consider it grounded?
predictThenReveal.answer:
It prints:
policy-refunds
grounded

The policy document contains the key terms "refund" and "deadline" context, so it should be selected before generation. In a real RAG system this check becomes a retrieval metric, not the whole answer-quality test.

decisionDoc.title: Decision prompts for Reranking for Better Answers

questions.q: What decision does Reranking for Better Answers change for a retriever finds many plausible docs and a reranker must put the truly useful evidence first?
questions.why: The lesson is valuable only if it changes an artifact, release gate, or evaluation tied to relevant evidence in the top three chunks.
questions.rot: Prefer the smallest design that exposes the failure case: reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents.

spans.text: From memory, reconstruct Reranking for Better Answers as a five-part path: the concrete problem (a retriever finds many plausible docs and a reranker must put the truly useful evidence first), the mechanism, the design choice, the implementation or verification check, and the failure mode (reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents). Then name the metric that tells you whether the work improved: relevant evidence in the top three chunks.

checklist.label: Can you state the running problem without using buzzwords?
Does your artifact show inputs, decision rule, output, and evidence?
Did you choose the smallest design that can improve relevant evidence in the top three chunks?
Will your tests catch this failure: reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents?
Have you named the next rung after the first reliable version ships?

capstone.prompt: Create a one-page plan for reranking experiment with baseline top-k, reranked top-k, and answer quality checks. Include the problem, inputs, mechanism, design choice, runnable or reviewable check, metric (relevant evidence in the top three chunks), known failure (reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents), and the next rung you would study or build after this lesson.
